title: Recording fidelity and the drummer Fats Martin
summary: Albert thinks the 1936 record was true to the band's sound though today sections could be separated; the Troy Floyd records were the same.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: What about in the 1936 session with your own band? How would it pick up the band? Do you think it picked up the drums fully?
Yeah, but I've never heard Fats Martin in person. Do you think it's fair to Fats Martin or fair to the rest of the band? Is it true to the band's sound is what I'm getting at?
I think it is. Yeah. But however, it could be, it would make a lot better today.
Yeah, it would be high fidelity today.

Why sure, why sure. You could cut each section out. Why is on this particular record, you have to let it play like it is. You can't show the reeds, you can't show the brass, you can't show the drums as you're referring to individually, which you can do today.
And what about in the Troy Floyd days?
It really didn't, it wasn't high fidelity, but it would pick up pretty much the sound.
Same thing because this is only, you're only talking about a year or two difference. Mm-hmm.
